articles.headline: OFAC Designates New Entities and Individuals in Latest Iran-Related Sanctions Action
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. This action targets entities and individuals deemed to be involved in activities supporting the Iranian regime.

These designations aim to further restrict the Iranian government's access to financial resources and its ability to engage in destabilizing activities. The specific individuals and entities added to the Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List were not immediately detailed in the initial announcement but are expected to be involved in various sectors supporting the Iranian economy or its illicit activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Imposes New Cyber-Related and Transnational Criminal Organization Sanctions, Alongside Cuba Designations
body: On November 5, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a series of new designations targeting cyber-related malicious activities and transnational criminal organizations. These actions aim to disrupt illicit financial networks and cyber threats that pose a risk to U.S. national security.

In a separate but concurrent action, OFAC also issued new designations related to Cuba and published a Cuba-related determination. The specifics of these designations and the determination were not immediately released but are expected to further tighten economic pressure on the Cuban government.

articles.headline: OFAC Expands Iran Sanctions, Updates Listings, and Amends Venezuela-Related General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 4, 2026, alongside updates to existing Iran-related listings. This move is part of ongoing efforts to exert economic pressure on Iran.

In conjunction with these actions, OFAC also published an Iran-related alert to provide guidance on potential evasion tactics. Furthermore, an amended Venezuela-related General License and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) were issued, signaling adjustments to U.S. policy concerning Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License FF-1 for International Development Bank for Investment and Finance
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of Iran General License FF-1 on October 29, 2026. This amended general license authorizes the wind down of transactions involving the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance.

The issuance of General License FF-1 indicates a specific, time-limited authorization for certain activities that would otherwise be prohibited under Iran sanctions. This allows for an orderly cessation of business with the designated entity, minimizing unintended disruptions while maintaining the overall sanctions regime.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates New Entities and Individuals Under North Korea and DRC Sanctions Programs
body: On October 28, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations under its North Korea sanctions program. These actions target individuals and entities involved in activities that support the North Korean regime's illicit weapons programs or other destabilizing actions.

Concurrently, OFAC also issued new designations related to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These designations aim to address corruption, human rights abuses, or other illicit activities undermining stability in the DRC.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a $1,529,685 settlement with Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, on October 27, 2026. The settlement resolves nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and services from the United States to Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA was blocked by operation of law due to its majority ownership by the designated JSC Concern Almaz-Antey.

OFAC determined that the violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious, citing reckless disregard for U.S. sanctions and substantial harm to U.S. foreign policy objectives. The Department of Justice also resolved a parallel investigation, with Extreme Networks agreeing to a non-prosecution agreement and criminal penalties.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: On October 26, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) amended 11 of its Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) concerning blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. This update is part of an ongoing review to ensure guidance remains current.

The revised FAQs, including numbers 10, 32-36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53, clarify when financial institutions must freeze funds, when a prohibited transaction should be rejected, and the procedures and deadlines for reporting these actions to OFAC.
Key changes include emphasizing the use of the OFAC Reporting System (ORS) for all filings and providing updated examples to distinguish between a customer inquiry and an actual payment instruction.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran and Russia General Licenses, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: On October 21, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations as part of 'Operation Economic Outcast,' targeting Iran's shadow fleet networks.

In a significant development, OFAC also removed certain individuals and entities from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List under the Belarus and North Korea sanctions programs. Specifically, Chinese national Lu Hezheng and two Chinese entities (Shanghai Moxing Cultural Media Co. Ltd. and Shanghai Hongman Cartoon and Animation Design Studio) were delisted from the North Korea program, and Belarusian national Andrei Alekseevich Rybakov was delisted from the Belarus program.
Furthermore, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended several Frequently Asked Questions, indicating adjustments to existing sanctions policies for these regions.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations and Issues Associated General Licenses
body: On October 19, 2026, the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations target individuals and entities involved in the theft or misappropriation of American intellectual property.

Alongside these designations, OFAC also issued associated General Licenses. These licenses are intended to provide specific authorizations for certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited, aiming to mitigate unintended consequences while upholding the objectives of the PAIPA sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and Issues New FAQ
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of an amended Venezuela-related General License on October 16, 2026. This amendment modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Venezuela.

In conjunction with the amended General License, OFAC also published a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) to provide further clarity and guidance on the scope and application of the updated authorization. This action reflects ongoing adjustments to U.S. sanctions policy concerning Venezuela.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Fined $1,529,685 by OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations. The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the settlement on October 27, 2026.

The violations, which occurred between September 2018 and March 2022, involved nine instances of exporting networking equipment and services from the United States to Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA). MMZA, a Russian defense manufacturer, was blocked by operation of law due to its majority ownership by the designated JSC Concern Almaz-Antey.

OFAC determined the violations were egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed. The company also resolved a parallel investigation with the Department of Justice, entering into a non-prosecution agreement and agreeing to criminal penalties.

articles.headline: Bank of America Fined $11,662,930 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to pay $11,662,930 to settle 475 apparent violations of various U.S. sanctions programs, as announced by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 13, 2026.

The violations, which occurred between September 2021 and April 2025, involved transactions related to Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism. OFAC classified the violations as non-egregious and mostly not voluntarily disclosed.

This settlement was part of a coordinated enforcement action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also included significant penalties from FinCEN and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) for anti-money laundering failures.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Pays $175,015 OFAC Penalty for Illicit Drug Trade Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarder, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle apparent violations of the Illicit Drug Trade Sanctions Regulations and OFAC's Reporting, Procedures and Penalties Regulations. The settlement was announced by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on October 9, 2026.

The violations involved facilitating the importation of a packet-filling machine from Youli Technology Development Co., Ltd., a Chinese supplier designated under Executive Order 14059 for selling pill presses to counterfeit-pill makers. Pegasus failed to identify Youli as a blocked entity after it changed its name, screening only the new name.

Additionally, Pegasus failed to respond fully to an OFAC administrative subpoena for six months. OFAC deemed the conduct non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, but noted mitigating factors such as no prior enforcement history and extensive remedial commitments.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $1,427,230 by OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has agreed to pay $1,427,230 to settle apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations, as announced by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on September 10, 2026.

The specifics of the violations were not detailed in the public record but typically involve transactions with sanctioned countries, entities, or individuals. OFAC regularly pursues enforcement actions against individuals who violate sanctions laws, underscoring the importance of compliance for all U.S. persons, regardless of their professional capacity.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems Settles with OFAC for $60,764 Over Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc., a Wisconsin-based manufacturer, has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle eight apparent violations of U.S. sanctions on Iran. The settlement was announced by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on August 12, 2026.

The violations stemmed from indirect sales of weighing equipment to an Iranian client through a Dubai-based distributor by Rice Lake's Italian subsidiary, Dini Argeo S.r.l., between June 2019 and November 2021. These sales occurred after the revocation of General License H, which had previously authorized such transactions.

OFAC determined the violations were non-egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, leading to a reduced penalty. The case highlights the importance of robust compliance programs for foreign subsidiaries of U.S. companies, especially when dealing with high-risk jurisdictions.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Pays $1,050,000 to OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: FTI Consulting, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,050,000 to settle apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations, as announced by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on June 1, 2026.

The details of the violations were not immediately made public but typically involve transactions or dealings with sanctioned countries, entities, or individuals. This enforcement action underscores OFAC's continued focus on ensuring compliance across various industries, including professional services firms.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Fined $275,000,000 by OFAC for Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL), an India-based multinational company, has agreed to pay $275,000,000 to settle 32 apparent violations of OFAC's Iran sanctions regulations. The settlement was announced by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on May 18, 2026.

Between November 2023 and June 2025, AEL purchased shipments of liquified petroleum gas (LPG) from a Dubai-based trader, which purported to supply Omani and Iraqi gas but actually originated from Iran. AEL caused U.S. financial institutions to process 32 U.S. dollar-denominated payments totaling approximately $192,104,044 for these shipments.

OFAC determined that AEL's apparent violations were egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, citing numerous red flags that should have alerted the company to the Iranian origin of the LPG. However, AEL received credit for its extensive cooperation and remedial measures taken after discovering the conduct.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities, Inc. Pays $1,110,661 to OFAC for Sanctions Violations
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,110,661 to settle apparent violations of U.S. sanctions regulations, as announced by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on March 17, 2026.

The specifics of the violations were not immediately detailed in the public record but typically involve failures in sanctions screening or processing transactions involving sanctioned parties. This enforcement action highlights the importance of robust compliance programs for financial institutions and trading platforms.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $3,777,000 by OFAC for Syrian Sanctions Violations
body: An individual residing abroad has agreed to pay $3,777,000 to settle 20 apparent violations of the Syrian Sanctions Regulations, as announced by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on February 25, 2026.

The violations occurred between 2018 and 2021 and involved prohibited transactions related to Syria. This significant penalty underscores OFAC's commitment to enforcing sanctions against individuals who engage in illicit activities with sanctioned regimes.

articles.headline: IMG Academy Fined $1,720,000 by OFAC for Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Violations
body: IMG Academy, LLC, a U.S.-based academic and athletic training institution, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle apparent violations of the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Sanctions Regulations. The settlement was announced by the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on February 12, 2026.

Over a five-year period, IMG Academy entered into tuition enrollment agreements with two individuals designated under the Kingpin Act and processed 89 related financial transactions for the benefit of the designees' children.

OFAC found that routine due diligence, such as screening contracting parties or payors, would have revealed that the individuals' names matched entries on the SDN List. Aggravating factors included reckless disregard for sanctions requirements and actual knowledge of transactional activity with sanctioned parties.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.
